# A census of Arbor's tests

<!-- Generated by `scripts/census.py --write` from scripts/census-template.md. Change the words there and the judgements in the script's tables, never here. -->

Some {{attributes}} tests pass, and the serious faults of late were all found on a real Mac. This census asks why that can be: which
tests could **never** fail on account of what macOS really does, what each kind of test proves, how much of the code that
talks to macOS anything runs at all, and which features a person would be hurt by that nothing has yet tried on a Mac.

**Taken at commit `{{commit}}`**, the last that changed anything it reads. Every number in sections 1 to 3 comes out of one script that reads the sources as text and builds nothing:

```bash
scripts/census.py
scripts/census.py --write
scripts/census.py --out /tmp/census
scripts/census.py --show PeekControllerTests
scripts/census.py --sample 60 --seed 4
```

The first prints the tables, the second regenerates this page whole, the third also writes one row per test (`tests.tsv`), per test file, per helper and per
file of real code. `--show` says how a test or a suite was classified and through which helpers; `--sample` draws tests at random, with their bodies, to check by hand.

**It is not part of `make check` or of CI, on purpose.** What is a judgement and not a reading stands in tables in the script, to be argued with: which members of the
stand-ins stand for the world, which suites have a tool for a subject, what a recording would have to hold for a helper to
count as seen on a Mac, what a run must switch on to get into each file of real code, which defaults the ranking in section 4 goes by. The script stops when the sources have
outgrown a table (a stand-in has a public member it has not been told about; a source line its reading of the wiring rests on is gone; a default has changed). Then a person looks. So
the page is as old as the commit above: take it again after a change to the stand-ins, to the real-window runs or to what ships switched on.

## The answer in short

- **{{never_mac}} of {{functions}} test functions ({{never_mac_pct}}) cannot fail because of anything macOS does**: they never meet it. {{A}} are
  arithmetic, {{B}} try the test tools themselves, {{on_stand_ins}} run the real controller against stand-ins.
- Of those {{on_stand_ins}}, **{{D}} have the world act, and the world is the fake**. {{d_uncovered}} of them ({{d_uncovered_pct}}) rest on at least one
  report or answer that no committed recording of a Mac holds; {{d_weak}} on one that is either unrecorded or known to differ
  from the recording; {{d_borne_out}} only on what a recording bears out.
- **{{E}} test functions replay real behaviour**: {{real_traces}} recordings, all from one kind of hosted Mac, one version of macOS, one
  1024×768 display, made by an early build. No recording holds a window opening, a display coming or going, a Space, full
  screen, a switch between apps, a native tab, a key held down, or the permission being taken away.
- **{{F}} functions run real macOS code**, {{f_drawing}} of them drawing into bitmaps in memory. None calls the Accessibility API, receives
  or posts an event, registers a shortcut or puts a window on the screen.
- Of the {{mac_lines}} lines that only a Mac can run, **at least {{unrun_lines}} lines and {{unrun_branches}} branches are run by nothing automatic**: no
  test, and neither of the two real-window runs CI makes. That includes {{input_unrun_pct}} of the input layer: the event taps, the shortcuts, the
  pinch, the rectangle. Another {{part_lines}} lines are in files that an automatic run enters only in part.
- **What could hurt a person most is what is checked least** (section 4): the event taps and the shortcuts, which are on from the first launch and hold every event of the Mac, are
  switched off in both automatic runs.

## 1. What each test touches

Each `@Test` function is put into exactly one class by what its body touches, and the helpers it calls in its own test target,
followed by name up to five calls deep (a file's `makeHarness()`, a `Desk` with an `init`, a suite kept in a property, an
extension of `Harness`).

| Class | What it is | What it proves | What it takes on trust |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** pure | Values in, values out: trees, layout, geometry, parsing, settings, state machines | The arithmetic is right | That the question is the right one. macOS cannot make it fail, and need not |
| **B** a stand-in or a tool | The subject is the fake, the harness, the chaos lab, the trace recorder and replayer, benchmarks, or the repository's own text read as text | The instruments work | Nothing about Arbor on a Mac |
| **C** commands only | The real controller on stand-ins. Windows are opened; everything else is a command, a shortcut pressed and let go, or time passing | Given this arrangement, this command gives that tree, view, reply, overlay | That `setFrame` and `focus` do as told and are echoed as the fake echoes them |
| **D** the world acts | As C, and the test has macOS, an app or a hand do something, or tells the stand-in what macOS or an app will answer | **If** macOS reports this, in this order, Arbor copes | The *if*: the order and content of reports the fake makes up |
| **E** a recording | A trace from `collab/evidence/traces` is replayed against the controller | Today's Arbor copes with what that Mac reported and those apps answered on that day | That the layer below the seam would still make the same events of it |
| **F** real macOS code | Compiled only on macOS, calling AppKit, Carbon, CoreGraphics or Arbor's macOS-only types | That piece of real code does what the test looks at | - |
| **G** real files, sockets, processes, queues | POSIX and Dispatch for real, the same on macOS and Linux | The control socket, the state and settings files, the log, the lock, the scheduler | - |

Where a test touches several, the order of precedence is F, E, B, G, D, C, A.

**How they were counted.** The sources hold {{attributes}} `@Test` attributes. {{twins}} stand in the `#else` of an `#if os(macOS)` or
`#if canImport(…)` as `@Test(.disabled(…)) func sameName() {}`, so that Linux reports the test as skipped: the same function
written twice, counted once. That leaves {{functions}}. A parameterised test (`@Test(arguments:)`, {{parameterised}} of them) is one function
however many cases it runs. {{mac_only}} functions are compiled only on macOS: the {{F}} of class F, and {{mac_only_not_f}} that hand the Mac shell's helper tools to
the compiler (class B; a change in Apple's SDK could fail those). {{enabled_if}} carry `.enabled(if:)`; {{disabled}} are disabled on the platform they are written for. {{known_issue}} wraps
its finding in `withKnownIssue`: the chaos lab's random walks report a script nobody knows and do not fail on it.

**Reading it.**

- **A, {{A_pct}}.** The whole of `ArborCoreTests` but {{core_not_a}} functions. It is the firmest ground there is and it says nothing about a Mac.
  {{table:decisions}}
  So the decisions of the two layers nearest to macOS are well tried *as decisions*; whether macOS sends what they are fed is
  the same open question as in class D, one level down.
- **C, {{C_pct}}.** The world holds still. {{c_clock}} of them let time pass; {{c_open_after}} open a window after the start, which by the definition used here is
  set-up, though it is a report like any other (table 2 counts it). Every one of them also meets the fake's echoes, which
  `Harness.run` delivers after each command.
- **D, {{D_pct}}.** The largest class. In {{d_reports}} the fake (or the test itself, calling the controller's event methods) sends a report or a hand works one of
  Arbor's panels; in {{d_answers}} the test only tells a stand-in what to answer (a minimum size, where the pointer is, what the Mac's facts are); {{d_walks}} are
  random walks of the chaos lab. {{d_helper_only}} are in D only through a helper: a `makeHarness()` that ends with `userFocus`, say.
- **E, {{E}} functions.** Each runs once per trace, {{traces}} cases each, and the second cuts every trace before every stimulus, which
  makes some three thousand states. It is the one headless kind that holds real behaviour, and it holds it as a fossil: it fails
  when Arbor changes, never when macOS does.
- **F, {{F_pct}}.** See table 1a. **G, {{G_pct}}** is real and is the same on both platforms; nothing in it is about windows.

{{f_files_none}} of the {{f_files}} files reach none of Arbor's own macOS-only code: they compare a table in `ArborCore` with Apple's constants (key codes,
scroll phases, menu key equivalents), which is worth having, or try the off-screen bitmap tool itself. `EventTapThreadTests` tries the thread and a tap that is never started. Two files read

### How far the classifier can be trusted

It reads text. It does not know types, so it follows names: a bare call to a member of the enclosing suite, then to the file,
then to the target; `.name` to the test target's types that have been named so far, and to its extensions of other
people's types; overloads by their argument labels. What a helper does is held against every test that reaches it,
whether or not that branch of the helper runs.

Checked by hand at commit `a391fe4`, each test read with its helpers, against the definitions above:

| Round | Drawn | Read | Wrong class | What was wrong, and what became of it |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | seed 1, eight from each class | 50 | 1 | A restart after a crash counted as the world acting (`restartedAfterAccident`). It is Arbor's own life: taken off the list, with what the memory store is told it found |
| 2 | seed 2, from all | 60 | 1 | A test that only compares paths counted as real files. Class G now wants a file read, written, made or removed |
| 3 | seed 3, from all | 60 | 0 | |
| 4 | seed 4, from all | 60 | 0 | One right class for a wrong reason (`controller.shortcut(for:)`, a question, taken for a key going down): mended |

**Two wrong in 230 (0.9 %). None in the last 120**, whose classes are the same under the final rules as when they were read; by the rule of
three that puts the error rate below 2.5 % with 95 % confidence. A seed draws other tests once a test has been added or removed, so the rounds can be
drawn again only at that commit.

Random samples were not what found the large mistakes. Reading the table per file, and three sweeps aimed at the classifier's weak
spots (calls in classes A and C that resolve to nothing known; helpers that have the world act and are not reached; tests in D only through a
helper), found these, all mended before round 3: 92 pure tests taken for D because a pure function has a `minimumSize:` label too; some
70 taken for G because private types of the same name in different files were merged; a dozen whose helper lives in another suite kept in a
property; seven where a loop that copies the windows of one run of Arbor into the next was taken for windows closing; four
`scenariosCan…` tests whose subject is the `expect` language; chaos scripts written on one line. `scripts/census.py --self-test` holds the script to most of these on small sources.

**Soft spots that remain.** Whether a suite's subject is a tool is a judgement (the list is in the script; {{b_listed}} functions hang on
it). "Answers only" is the softest edge of D: a `makeHarness()` that puts the pointer somewhere makes the tests about the look of tiles class D. Budget
tests that go through `BenchmarkCase` are in B as benchmarks, though what they pin is the controller's thrift. A test that gets a saved
state out of a harness and then only decodes it is C.

## 2. Class D: what the fake is trusted with

For each helper that stands for the world: how many tests rest on it, and whether what it reports has ever been held against a recording of a real
Mac. The evidence looked for:

- **Recordings**: `collab/evidence/traces/*.jsonl`. For each helper the script names the kind of line a recording would have to hold
  (`setFullScreen`: a `changed` whose window says `fullScreen`; `setDisplays`: a `displaysChanged` after which a display has come, gone, moved or
  changed size, not merely lost two points to the Dock) and lists the traces from a Mac that hold one.
- **Known differences**: the table "What real macOS does that `FakeWindowSystem` does not" in the traces' README, for the rows where the fake, read today,
  still does otherwise.
- **Citations**: comments in `Sources/ArborTesting` and `FaithfulFakeTests`, which pins the fake's order of reports. Both cite
  `collab/evidence/ax-events.txt`. **That file is not in the repository**, so what they cite cannot be checked from here.
- **Outcomes on real windows**: whether `arbor-e2e` or `e2e-drag.sh`, which CI runs on a Mac, bring the same situation about. They check where windows end up,
  not what macOS reported on the way: a sign that Arbor copes, no check of the fake.
- **Real input once**: `collab/evidence/gestures-latest.txt`, one run of `proof.sh` (table 2d).

"report": the fake, or the test itself, sends Arbor an event. "answer": the test tells a stand-in what to say when asked. "panel": a hand on one of Arbor's own
panels, played by calling the action the real panel would call.

**Reading it.**

- **`userFocus` carries {{d:system.userFocus}} of the {{D}} tests of class D.** A recording holds a focus report after a press, within one app. None holds a switch from one app to another, which the
  helper stands for as well; there the fake announces the app and then the window, once each, while its own comments say that macOS reports a focus that crosses apps
  two to four times.
- **A window opening is in no recording.** {{d:system.open}} tests of class D ({{all:system.open}} of all classes) open one while Arbor runs. The order the fake uses (appeared, then focused) is pinned by
  `FaithfulFakeTests` to a file that is not here. CI does open windows on a real Mac and looks at where they end up.
- **Displays are the largest premise with nothing behind it at all**: {{d:system.setDisplays}} tests on `setDisplays` and {{d:system.displayList=}} on a silent change of the list, no recording, no real-window run in CI
  (`check-displays.sh` plugs in a virtual display, when somebody starts it). What the recordings have under `displaysChanged` is the Dock growing by two points.
- **Keys held down** ({{d:harness.keyDown}} and {{d:harness.keyUp}} tests), **typing** ({{d:system.type}}), **Spaces** ({{d:system.setOnActiveSpace}}), **the permission** ({{d:harness.watchAccessibility}}, {{d:harness.revokeAccessibility}}, {{d:harness.grantAccessibility}}, {{d:controller.accessibilityGranted=}}): no recording, and no automatic run has shortcuts switched on.
- **Full screen** ({{d:system.setFullScreen}}), **an app that comes forward** ({{d:system.comesForward}}), **an app that hangs** ({{d:system.setUnresponsive}}), **native tabs** ({{d:system.openTab}}): no recording; `arbor-e2e` does bring each about. In the one run of `proof.sh` on record,
  full screen came out {{claim:a docked window goes full screen and comes back}} and the app coming forward {{claim:switching to an app whose window is out of view}}.
- Where there *is* a recording it has earned its keep: the helpers of table 2b are known to differ because somebody could look. Drags are the plainest case: {{d:system.drag}} tests use a `drag`
  that begins before the window moves and never focuses, and {{found:system.drag}} recordings show a drag that begins a third of a second late, on a window that has already moved and, if it did not have the keyboard, has been focused first.
- The recordings are one kind of Mac on one day. A premise marked "recorded" has been seen once, on test windows or five stock apps, on macOS 26.6.2 at 1024×768.

## 3. The other side: real code and who runs it

Every file that only a Mac can run or that stands at the edge: lines of code (not blank, not only a comment), branches (`if`, `guard`, `while`, each `case` and `default` of a `switch`; not
`??`, `?:` or `catch`), and what executes it.

**Automatic** means: CI does it without being asked, as `.github/workflows/ci.yml` stands. That is `swift test` on a Mac (class F) and on both platforms (class G, the smoke scripts), and the job `real-windows`, which runs
`arbor-e2e --full-screen` and `scripts/mac-shell/e2e-drag.sh`. The two macOS jobs are left out when `scripts/ci-changes.py` finds that a Mac could prove nothing new. **By hand** means a Mac shell script
that runs only when somebody starts it (`workflow_dispatch`).

**How it was read.** There is no coverage measurement, so this is a reading of the wiring. Both automatic runs start the real app with `ARBOR_NO_HOTKEYS=1`, `ARBOR_NO_STATUS_ITEM=1`,
`ARBOR_NO_PROMPT=1` and `ARBOR_ONLY_PIDS=…`, on hosted Macs that come with Reduce Motion on. For each file the script holds what a run must switch on or send to get into it at all, and asks
each run and each script whether it does. A file that an automatic run gets into counts as run **whole**. For class F the names a test reaches are followed on into the sources, member by member, and whatever is reached
counts whole as well. Both are generous, so **the lines nothing runs are a lower bound**.

**Reading it.**

- **The input layer is dark.** {{input_unrun}} of its {{input_lines}} lines and {{input_unrun_branches}} of its {{input_branches}} branches run only when somebody starts a script: `HotKeyCenter`, `GestureTap`, `RectangleFramer`, `PointerInput`, `DesktopProbe`, `WindowList`, and in
  `EventTap` everything from installing a tap to its callback. One switch does it: both automatic runs set `ARBOR_NO_HOTKEYS=1`. These are the callbacks macOS holds every event of the system for.
  Their decisions are among the best tried code there is ({{a_decisions}} pure tests); that an event ever reaches them is checked by `input-taps.sh`, by hand.
- **What a person touches first is dark too**: the menu bar item ({{unrun:UI/StatusMenu.swift}} lines), the welcome window's own half ({{unrun:UI/Onboarding.swift}}), the name field ({{unrun:UI/NamePanel.swift}}), the minimap's panel ({{unrun:UI/MinimapPanel.swift}}), the stage that plays every motion ({{unrun:UI/Stage.swift}}, because
  the hosted Macs reduce motion), the update window ({{unrun:UI/UpdateWindow.swift}}).
- **`CallSensor` ({{unrun:App/CallSensor.swift}} lines) is run by nothing whatever**: not under `ARBOR_ONLY_PIDS`, and no script switches its settings on. They ship off.
- **"Automatic, in part" is where the weight is.** `AXWindowSystem.swift`, {{loc:AX/AXWindowSystem.swift}} lines and {{branches:AX/AXWindowSystem.swift}} branches, {{branches_pct:AX/AXWindowSystem.swift}} of all the branches in the macOS-only code, is entered by both runs, with a handful of test windows of one obliging app (and a second app for a
  moment) on one display. Whatever only other apps, a second display, Spaces or a slow Mac bring about in it is not entered, and nothing says how much that is. `compat.sh` puts thirteen stock apps in front of it, by hand.
- **Entered is not looked at.** The runs compare frames with the window server's and see that some panels are there. Nothing automatic clicks a tile, drags a gap handle, types into Go to… or the settings window, or looks at the hint that shows after the first real dock.
- **The edge that is well covered** is the one that is not macOS: the control socket ({{g:IPC/ControlServer.swift}} and {{g:IPC/ControlEndpoint.swift}} tests of class G, both real-window runs, two smoke scripts).

## 4. Features and what has been seen of them on a Mac

Sections 1 to 3 count tests and lines. This one asks the same of features: which have no check on real windows at all, which have one that nobody runs automatically, which have one that has never
run; **ranked by how much a person would be hurt if the feature misbehaved on a real Mac**. It is a reading by a person, not a count: the words are in the template, and the script only
holds it to the facts it goes by: the defaults in `Settings.swift`, which commands have a default shortcut, that every script named exists, and that what stands between quotation marks is still said by a spec, a step or a comment.

**The measure**, in this order:

1. **What the worst fault does.** **1**: input blocked for the whole Mac; a window lost, hidden or stuck; something moved that nobody moved. **2**: a jolt, the wrong window, a wrong view, keys that go to the wrong place. **3**: cosmetic.
2. **Is it within reach as Arbor ships?** *always* (it works from the first launch without being asked) and *key* (on a default shortcut) count alike; then *menu*: an item of the menu; *asked for*: only by a setting, a shortcut of one's own or `arborctl`; *off*: ships switched off.
3. **Has its macOS half ever run on a Mac?** *never*, by the spec's own words; *not said*; *in part* (an earlier state, other keys, by command and not by hand); *yes*.
4. **Does CI run a check of it?** *no*; *in part* (by command, where a person uses a key or the pointer; or a step that cannot fail); *yes*.

Ties go first to what is known to fail today, then to what is met more often. **Where the facts are from**: each spec's status line and Shipped note in `docs/features/`, read at the commit above; `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; and the runs made on hosted Macs on 2026-10-14 (macOS 26.6.2, one 1024×768 display), whose
outputs are not committed: given as passed/failed. Several specs still say that their macOS half has not been compiled: since CI builds everything on a hosted Mac, that much is out of date for all of them, and *never* below means never run.

### No real-window check exists at all

- **Built, and within reach**: F11 (no rule has ever placed a real window), F25 (a display's name and kind come from macOS and have not been seen), F33 (but for `gapHandles`), F35 (places kept for windows on other Spaces: built, though its
  status line says "ready"; its criterion 6 is a script still to write), F57 on test windows (rank 6).
- **Built, and needs none**: F62 ("Nothing here is macOS-only"). F50's shipped parts and F28's replays are headless by nature; every Mac shell script uses `arborctl`, and `trace-demo.sh` records.
- **Not built**: F04, F14, F34, F52, F59.

### A check exists and has never run, by the spec's own words

F08, F13, F20, F22, F26, F41, F44 (with real keys), F49, F51, F53, F55, F58, F60 (the guard), F63; and `shots-finder.sh`, the half of F27 that presses keys. All but the guard can be reached as Arbor ships; F51, F55 and F63 work from the first launch.

### Ships off until seen

`guardDesktopClicks` (F60), `continuousZoom` (F16), `windowPictures` (F02), `minimapDuration` 0 (F26), `holdStillWhileCameraIsOn` and `holdStillWhileMicrophoneIsOn` (F58), `soleFloatTakesDesktop` (F18), `newWindows` "float" (F23),
`reflowWhileDragging` (F09), `tabsEnabled` (F04), `automaticUpdateChecks` (F13). That is the right default for what nobody has seen. **The same rule was not applied to `peek`, `scrollZoom` and the ⌃⌥ rectangle**, which by their specs have been seen no more
and ship on.

## What the numbers suggest

1. **The suite proves "if macOS says this, Arbor copes", {{D}} times, and checks the *if* in {{real_traces}} recordings.** Faults found on a Mac are what that shape predicts. More tests of class D add nothing on that side.
2. **A recording is the cheapest thing that turns a premise into a fact**, and it stays a test. By table 2a the first to make: a window opening (in an app that runs, and in one that starts), a second display plugged in and out, a switch between two apps by ⌘Tab and
   by click, a shortcut held and let go, a Space, full screen, a tab, a hang. `trace-demo.sh` is the pattern, and today's build would also record the answers to the questions the old one did not ask.
3. **`collab/evidence/ax-events.txt` should be in the repository or stop being cited.** `FaithfulFakeTests` holds the fake to it.
4. **One more automatic session with the switches off** (`ARBOR_NO_HOTKEYS=0`, `ARBOR_NO_STATUS_ITEM=0`, Reduce Motion off) on the hosted Mac, with a few real keys, one pinch, one ⌃⌥-drag and one click in the menu bar, would bring most of the {{unrun_lines}} lines under an automatic run, and the first two ranks of table 4 with them. The scripts exist.
5. **Fourteen features have a check that is written and has never run.** Running each once on a hosted Mac is the largest gain for the least work on this page.
6. **Measure instead of reading.** Table 3 is an argument from the wiring. The real-window job could build Arbor with coverage instrumentation and publish what the two runs really execute; `AXWindowSystem.swift` is where that would tell most.
